name: Preparedness paradox
statement: Preparation that works leaves no disaster to point at, so the money it cost is judged afterwards as an overreaction.
meaning: Two separable claims sit inside the name. The first is about perception: harm that was prevented leaves nothing for anyone to weigh against the cost, so the cost stands alone and looks excessive. The second is about incentives: officials who expect that reading spend on visible response rather than on invisible prevention. No experiment on the first claim was located. The second has been put to randomised tests, and they do not support its strong form. The name also carries at least four other ideas in print. Ruggiero and Vos give it to the tension between preparing the public through information and the official assumption that the public will panic. In business and disaster research a preparedness paradox is usually the gap between how worried people say they are and how little they do about it. In epidemiology the near-identical prevention paradox belongs to Geoffrey Rose and means something else again. In pandemic research a paradox usually names low uptake of a precaution during an outbreak, as in the 2009 H1N1 vaccination rates studied by Reintjes and colleagues across the Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, Spain and the United Kingdom.

origin.who: Chris Hayes, quoting a doctor he did not name
origin.note: The claim in its present form spread in March 2020 under the name 'paradox of preparation'. Jason Kottke quoted Hayes on 16 March 2020: the only way to get ahead of the curve is to take actions that at the time seem like overreactions. Hayes was replying to the physician James Hamblin, who had written that effective shutdowns would look in retrospect like unnecessary overreactions. The phrase 'preparedness paradox' is much older. A Google Books snippet of the United States Senate Committee on Armed Services hearings of July 1949 on an easement for a toll crossing of San Francisco Bay carries, at page 79, the words 'preparedness paradox that continually confronts the military planners. On one hand, we are constantly aware of the tremendous expense of military preparedness'. The snippet does not show who is speaking, so the attribution to General Bradley rests on the quotation Wikipedia prints rather than on anything read here. Ruggiero and Vos used the phrase in a journal in 2014. The earliest title carrying it that a Crossref title search returns is Kruger, Fernandes, Cupal and Homish in 2019, whose abstract could not be obtained.

evidence: The claim about perception has not been tested directly. What has been measured is the political half, and those results pull apart. Healy and Malhotra used data on natural disasters, government spending and election returns in the United States, and report that voters reward the incumbent presidential party for delivering disaster relief spending but not for investing in preparedness. They estimate that $1 spent on preparedness is worth about $15 in future damage mitigated. That sentence is read from the abstract deposited at Crossref and shown at Cambridge University Press, the full text having not been obtained, so no coefficients are quoted. Three randomised experiments since then complicate the picture. Bechtel and Mannino fielded a quota sample of 2,618 American citizens through Respondi in October 2016 and asked each to split $100 million between preparedness and relief. Telling respondents that preparedness cuts future damage raised the preparedness share by $5.25 million, standard error 0.91, against a control baseline of $44.43 million. Their text rounds that to about $6 million, a rise of 13 per cent, which the table does not quite support. A prime that only mentioned relief moved nothing, 0.26 with standard error 0.88. Support for a local flood control dam rose 4 percentage points when its cost was set at $2 million rather than $14 million, and by 1.7 points at $8 million, which was not statistically significant. Weller and Jamieson ran two preregistered survey experiments on 3,414 respondents, 1,595 recruited through Qualtrics between 29 June and 14 July 2021 and 1,819 through Amazon Mechanical Turk between 4 and 6 April 2022, about 900 to each condition. Information that better preparation would have saved lives in the covid-19 pandemic raised support for preparedness spending, for public health spending in general and for an incumbent proposing it. Their other two treatments did not behave as predicted. A treatment about the opioid epidemic did not raise support for public health spending, and one about a decline in spending at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention raised support for pandemic preparedness, which the authors had expected it not to do. The effects are drawn as coefficient plots with 95 per cent intervals and the text prints no point estimates. Among respondents who doubted that public health spending works, three of four treatment effects were significant and the fourth was positive and short of significance. Kim, Cragun and DeScioli put a fictional flood-prone community to 397 people on Mechanical Turk and found no greater support for relief than for prevention. The Atlas carries their design and figures at entry 543. Gissing, Van Leeuwen, Tofa and Haynes surveyed the central business district of Lismore in New South Wales, where a levee built in 2005 for $21 million protects against floods up to a one-in-ten-year event. Fifty of about 400 flood-prone businesses answered by telephone in November 2016 and February 2017. Thirty-two per cent expected to flood less often than once a decade, which overstates what the levee was built to do. Thirty-four per cent said preparing mattered less than it had before the levee. Eighty per cent had a flood action plan, against 97% of the 73 questionnaires completed in 2002. The levee overtopped for the first time in March 2017, and of 15 businesses asked afterwards, 14 said the community had grown less prepared since it went up.

replication.headline: The judgement the name describes has not been tested, and the political claim under it has, with survey experiments and election data disagreeing.
replication.detail: Nothing found measures the first claim, that averted harm is judged afterwards as harm that was never coming. Searching on 21 September 2026 covered Crossref by title and by bibliographic text, Europe PMC, PubMed, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, Google Books and open web search. OpenAlex refused every query for want of daily quota. Under other names the second claim has been tested. Kim, Cragun and DeScioli gave 397 Mechanical Turk participants a fictional flood-prone community in April 2020 in a design crossing three policies with two levels of citizen cooperation. Where the citizens were cooperative, support did not differ across relief, relief preparation and prevention. Where they were uncooperative, relief drew less support than prevention, t(121) = 2.95, p = 0.0038, which the authors call the opposite of what previous research predicted. Bechtel and Mannino and Weller and Jamieson both find that describing what preparedness achieves moves people towards funding it, which is hard to square with an electorate that cannot value prevention at all. Healy and Malhotra's election returns sit on the other side, and they measure votes rather than any judgement of a counterfactual. The hazards literature tests the nearest thing to the perception claim under the heading of near misses. Dillon, Tinsley and Cronin report that people given information about a past hurricane that passed without damage were less likely to buy flood insurance, in the general population and among people with a professional interest in risk, and less likely to evacuate. Tinsley, Dillon and Cronin report the same pattern for hurricane evacuation, Caribbean cruises and deep-water drilling, and report it reversing when a near miss is put to people as a disaster that almost happened. Both papers are closed at their publishers and are quoted here from the abstracts their publishers deposited at Crossref. The phrase itself still pulls in other subjects. A Crossref title search returns seven papers carrying it, on life history theory, climate attitudes, business continuity, Zambian tourism, information technology operations, flood readiness in the United Arab Emirates and readiness for extreme rainfall in Hong Kong. A Europe PMC search on the phrase returns five records, none of them about this idea.

study.cite: Kim, H. H., Cragun, J., & DeScioli, P. (2026). Prevention or relief? Voters' support for disaster policies. Disasters, 50(1), e70016.

limits: The two cases the claim is usually argued from do not carry it. Y2K is the first. Quiggin puts world spending at as much as US$500 billion and Australian spending at A$12 billion, and reports that no serious evaluation after the event was made. His argument runs the other way. Problems were slight even where little remediation was done, Italy's official body first met in February 1999 and confined remediation to critical systems, and Eastern Europe largely ignored the problem without seeing the failures the standard account predicted. He also names the trap: the absence of any serious Y2K problems could always be attributed to the success of the remediation programme, so the claim cannot lose. He adds that incentives ran towards spending, because those who argued for fixing faults as they appeared faced blame for any failure while those who argued for comprehensive remediation faced little risk of loss, an asymmetry sharpened by the threat of litigation in the United States. The version read here is the February 2004 University of Queensland working paper; the published version appeared in the Australian Journal of Public Administration in 2005 and was not obtained. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic is the second. The review committee convened under the International Health Regulations, chaired by Harvey Fineberg, reported to the World Health Assembly on 5 May 2011 and dealt with the charge that WHO had overstated the danger. Its answer was that reasonable criticism can be based only on what was known at the time and not on what was later learnt. Of 899 patients hospitalised in Mexico between late March and 1 June 2009, 58 became critically ill, and 41% of those died. In August 2009 the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology in the United States sketched a scenario of 30,000 to 90,000 American deaths, and the committee reports that the midpoint and upper level turned out to be five times the post-pandemic estimate of the actual number. Even so, 87% of deaths were in people under 65. That is a forecast corrected by events rather than a disaster held off by preparation, and the committee nowhere credits the response with the mild outcome. It found no evidence of commercial influence on WHO decisions, and it found real faults, among them the absence of a consistent, measurable and understandable depiction of severity. Its lead conclusion was that the world is ill-prepared for a severe pandemic. Attempts to open the Council of Europe Parliamentary Assembly's pages on its own 2010 inquiry returned an error at the previous check and were not retried, so nothing is claimed here about what that body resolved. Four documents wanted for this entry could not be opened on 21 September 2026. Healy and Malhotra's full text is behind a paywall at Cambridge University Press, and the copy deposited in Loyola Marymount University's repository is served behind a bot challenge rather than a paywall. The abstract of Kruger and colleagues is absent from Crossref, closed at the publisher and held in no open repository that Unpaywall or Semantic Scholar knows of. Thompson's published article is closed at Wiley and only his preprint was read. Rose's 1981 paper was read in full at the previous check and could not be reopened this time, PubMed Central answering with a bot challenge, bmj.com with a 403 and the Europe PMC full-text service with an error.
misreadings: Rose's prevention paradox is a different idea, and merging the two is the commonest error. His 1981 paper in the BMJ puts it as a measure that brings large benefits to the community offers little to each participating individual. His examples are arithmetic rather than psychology. Mass diphtheria immunisation in Britain 40 years earlier took roughly 600 children immunised for one life saved. If all male British doctors wore seat belts on every journey of their working lives, about 400 would take the precaution for each life saved, and 399 would buckle up every day for 40 years without benefit to their survival. From the Framingham data, a man of average coronary risk who cut his serum cholesterol by 0.65 mmol/l for life had about a one in 50 chance of avoiding coronary heart disease before 55, one in 25 in a group with mild hypertension and smoking, and one in 400 and one in 150 for women in those two groups. Rose's conclusion is that individual health education will not motivate people, because there is little in it for each of them. Nothing in it concerns how averted harm is judged afterwards. The wording usually quoted, which inserts 'preventative' before 'measure', comes from the 2008 book Rose's Strategy of Preventive Medicine rather than from the 1981 paper, as Thompson's citation shows. The Lismore result belongs to a third idea again, called the levee effect or the safe development paradox, in which protective works lower readiness for the flood that eventually arrives. The Atlas treats the general form of that at entry 115, risk compensation, and the failure to act on a warning at entry 106, normalcy bias. Healy and Malhotra get cited as proof that preparation is punished. What they report is that relief is rewarded and preparedness is not, which is indifference rather than punishment, and their outcome is votes rather than any judgement about a counterfactual. Asked directly, in Kim, Cragun and DeScioli's experiment, people back prevention as readily as relief. Naming the pattern settles nothing about whether a given preparation was worth its price. Whether harm was averted is the point in dispute, and the paradox as usually stated assumes the answer.

The abstract was read at Crossref and at Cambridge Core and is the source for the $1 to $15 figure. The full text is paywalled at Cambridge Core, and the copy in Loyola Marymount University's repository returned a Cloudflare bot challenge on 21 September 2026.

Journal of Contingencies and Crisis Management, 23(3), 138-148, published online 29 September 2014. Read in full from the copy self-archived at the University of Jyvaskyla. It contains the sentence 'A preparedness paradox exists', used for the tension between empowering the public and the assumption that the public will panic.
Kottke, J. (2020, March 16). The paradox of preparation. kottke.org. The source for the Chris Hayes formulation.

Wikipedia. Preparedness paradox, revision of 12 January 2026, read as wikitext. Used only to locate candidate sources, among them the 1949 congressional hearing and the Ruggiero and Vos paper. Its attribution of the 1949 line to General Bradley is not carried by the snippet that was obtained.

Bechtel, M. M., & Mannino, M. (2023). Ready When the Big One Comes? Natural Disasters and Mass Support for Preparedness Investment. Political Behavior, 45(3), 1045-1070. Read in full as the publisher's open-access PDF. Source for the 2,618 respondents, the October 2016 fielding, the $5.25 million coefficient and the dam cost effects.

Source for the 397 participants, the April 2020 fielding and the t(121) = 2.95 comparison. The Atlas also cites it at entry 543.

Frontiers in Earth Science, 10, 847196. Read in full as the JATS XML. Cited for the hazards field's own name for the problem, invisible success, which it ties to outcome bias and answers with counterfactual modelling rather than with an experiment.
